pg-easy-01.syntax:
-- General form
--   expr1 || expr2
-- The operator is chosen by the operand types (operator overloading).
-- Postgres defines || for several type families (text, arrays, bytea, jsonb, tsvector...).

-- Example 1: building a label from columns
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM people;

-- Example 2: array operand
SELECT ARRAY[1,2] || 3;   -- appends an element to an array

-- Gotchas / variations
-- * NULL operand: with plain || the whole result is NULL.
--     SELECT 'a' || NULL;          -- yields NULL
--   concat(a, b, ...) skips NULLs; concat_ws(sep, a, b, ...) adds a separator.
-- * Non-text operand: one side may be a non-text type, which is cast to text.
--     SELECT 'n=' || 42;
--   With two untyped literals or two non-text values, add an explicit cast: 42::text.
-- * Precedence: || binds looser than + and -, so wrap mixed expressions in parentheses.
-- * Logical OR is the keyword OR, not a symbol.
-- * Bytea values use || too, joining the byte strings.
pg-easy-01.title: The || operator and operator semantics in Postgres

pg-easy-02.syntax:
-- General form
--   expr1 || expr2          -- operator form
--   concat(expr1, expr2, ...) -- function form
--   concat_ws(sep, expr1, expr2, ...) -- with separator

-- Examples
SELECT 'foo' || 'bar';               -- ordinary text concatenation
SELECT 'id-' || 42;                  -- non-text operand is converted to text
SELECT concat('x', NULL, 'y');       -- function form: see notes below
SELECT concat_ws('-', 'a', NULL, 'c'); -- separator form: see notes below

-- Gotchas
-- * The || operator is strict: most operators and functions
--   in Postgres that are strict return NULL when any input is NULL.
--   Think of NULL as "unknown value", so combining it with
--   anything stays unknown.
-- * concat() and concat_ws() are not strict: they treat NULL
--   arguments specially (check the docs for exact behavior).
-- * COALESCE(col, '') replaces NULL with a fallback before
--   using ||.
--   e.g. SELECT first || ' ' || COALESCE(middle, '') FROM people;
-- * Test for NULL with IS NULL, not = NULL.
-- * || also works on arrays and bytea, with the same
--   NULL-input considerations.
pg-easy-02.title: String concatenation and NULL handling

pg-easy-03.syntax:
-- General form
-- string LIKE pattern [ESCAPE escape_char]
-- string NOT LIKE pattern
-- Pattern wildcards: % = any sequence (including empty), _ = exactly one character
-- A pattern with no wildcards behaves like equality.

-- Examples
SELECT * FROM products WHERE sku LIKE 'AB_-%';      -- 'AB', any one char, '-', then anything
SELECT * FROM products WHERE title NOT LIKE '%sale%';

-- Related operators (PostgreSQL extensions / shorthand)
--   ~~   is LIKE        !~~  is NOT LIKE
--   ~~*  is the ILIKE-style variant   !~~* is NOT ILIKE
--   SIMILAR TO and ~ / ~* are different: they use regular-expression-style syntax

-- Escaping a literal wildcard
SELECT * FROM files WHERE path LIKE '100\%%';           -- default escape is backslash
SELECT * FROM files WHERE path LIKE '100#%%' ESCAPE '#'; -- custom escape character

-- Gotchas
-- * The pattern must match the WHOLE string, not just part of it.
-- * % and _ also match newline characters.
-- * NULL on either side yields NULL, not true or false.
-- * Leading wildcards ('%abc') generally prevent ordinary B-tree index use.
-- * Prefix searches on a B-tree need the right operator class (text_pattern_ops) in non-C locales.
-- * For substring or case-variant searches at scale, consider the pg_trgm extension with a GIN/GiST index.
pg-easy-03.title: Pattern matching with LIKE and related operators

pg-easy-04.syntax:
-- General form: \d<letter>[S+] [pattern]
--   S = include system objects, + = more detail (size, description)
--   pattern uses psql wildcards: * (any chars), ? (one char); schema.name allowed

-- Examples (different objects than the quiz):
\di              -- list indexes
\di+ *_idx       -- indexes ending in _idx, with size/description
\df public.*     -- functions in schema public

-- Common members of the family:
--   \d name   describe one relation (columns, indexes, constraints)
--   \d        list tables, views, sequences, materialized views, foreign tables
--   \dn       schemas
--   \di       indexes
--   \dv       views
--   \dm       materialized views
--   \ds       sequences
--   \df       functions
--   \du / \dg roles
--   \dt       tables
--   \l        databases
--   \dx       extensions
--   \dT       data types

-- Gotchas:
--  * Each letter selects ONE kind of object; read the letter as an abbreviation.
--  * Lists only objects on your search_path unless you give a pattern
--    like 'other_schema.*' or use \d*.*
--  * Meta-commands are psql features, not SQL; no trailing semicolon needed.
--  * Use \? inside psql to see the full list of commands.
pg-easy-04.title: psql object-listing meta-commands (\d family)

pg-easy-05.syntax:
-- General form (typed at the psql prompt, not SQL; no semicolon needed):
--   \<command> [pattern]
-- Meta-commands are handled by psql itself, not sent to the server.
-- Most "describe" commands start with \d and accept an optional name pattern.

-- Examples:
\dt sales.*      -- tables whose schema is 'sales'
\df *count*      -- functions whose name contains 'count'

-- Related families (letter after the backslash picks the object kind):
--   \dt   tables in the search path
--   \dv   views
--   \di   indexes
--   \ds   sequences
--   \dn   schemas
--   \du   roles (users and groups)
--   \df   functions
--   \d name   describe one relation (columns, indexes)
--   \conninfo show current connection details
--   \c dbname switch to another database
--   \?    list all meta-commands
--   \q    quit

-- Gotchas:
--   * Add + for more detail (e.g. \dt+ shows size, \du+ shows descriptions).
--   * Add S to include system objects (e.g. \dtS).
--   * Commands are case-sensitive: \dt and \DT differ.
--   * Patterns use * and ? wildcards, not SQL % and _.
--   * Under the hood they query system catalogs (pg_catalog); psql -E shows the SQL used.
--   * Some commands list server-wide things, others only the current database or schema search path.
pg-easy-05.title: psql backslash meta-commands for listing objects

pg-easy-07.syntax:
-- psql meta-commands start with a backslash and are handled by psql itself,
-- not sent to the server as SQL.
--   \q          quit psql (also \quit)
--   \conninfo   show current connection details
--   \set        show or set psql variables
--   \echo text  print text

-- Explicit transaction control is plain SQL sent to the server:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO audit_log(msg) VALUES ('hello');
-- choose one way to end the transaction:
COMMIT;      -- make changes permanent
-- ROLLBACK; -- discard changes

-- Gotchas (as comments):
-- * psql is only a client; the transaction lives on the server
--   and belongs to the connection.
-- * Think about what the server does when a connection
--   closes while a transaction is still open.
-- * Check state with the prompt: %x in PROMPT1 shows
--   '*' when in a transaction block, '!' when failed.
--     \set PROMPT1 '%/%x%R%# '
-- * \set AUTOCOMMIT off makes psql open a transaction
--   implicitly before your first command; you must
--   COMMIT explicitly.
-- * Ctrl-D (end of input) also ends the session, like \q.
pg-easy-07.title: psql meta-commands and transaction state at session end

pg-easy-08.syntax:
-- psql backslash meta-commands are handled by the psql client, not the server.
-- General form:
--   \command [argument]

-- Display-related toggles (no argument flips the current state):
--   \timing [on|off]    client-side timing of statements
--   \pset [option [value]]   set a table output option
--   \a                  toggle aligned / unaligned output
--   \H                  toggle HTML output
--   \x [on|off|auto]    toggle expanded output mode

-- Example session:
--   mydb=> \pset border 2
--   mydb=> \pset null '(null)'
--   mydb=> \pset format aligned

-- Gotchas:
-- * Calling a toggle with no argument flips it; passing on/off sets it explicitly.
-- * \pset with no arguments lists nothing; use \pset OPTION to show one setting.
-- * Settings last only for the current session unless placed in ~/.psqlrc.
-- * \x auto picks the layout per result, based on terminal width.
-- * Meta-commands end at the end of the line; they take no semicolon.
-- * Related: \pset pager, \pset columns, \pset format (aligned, csv, html, wrapped).
-- * Use \? inside psql to list all meta-commands.
pg-easy-08.title: psql meta-commands for output display formatting

pg-easy-10.syntax:
-- General form
-- column_name  SMALLSERIAL | SERIAL | BIGSERIAL  [constraints]
-- Each is shorthand (not a true type) that expands to:
--   CREATE SEQUENCE tbl_col_seq AS <int type>;
--   col <int type> NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval('tbl_col_seq');
--   ALTER SEQUENCE tbl_col_seq OWNED BY tbl.col;

-- Example 1: declare
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  label text
);

-- Example 2: the identity-column alternative (SQL standard)
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id   integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  note text
);

-- Underlying types and sequence ranges (check the docs table):
--   SMALLSERIAL -> smallint
--   SERIAL      -> integer
--   BIGSERIAL   -> bigint
-- Compare the storage size and range of each underlying type.

-- Gotchas
-- * Sequences do not roll back; gaps are normal.
-- * The sequence is created with the column's type, so its maximum matches that type.
-- * Exceeding the maximum raises an error on nextval.
-- * Dropping the column drops its owned sequence.
-- * Inspect: SELECT pg_get_serial_sequence('invoices','id');
-- * Foreign keys referencing the column should use the matching plain type (bigint/integer), not serial.
pg-easy-10.title: Auto-incrementing column types (serial pseudo-types)

docs.title: SQL Syntax: Identifiers and Key Words

pg-easy-12.syntax:
-- General form:
--   unquoted_identifier   -> case-insensitive name
--   "Quoted Identifier"   -> exact name, case and spaces preserved

-- Example 1: unquoted names
CREATE TABLE Orders (OrderId int, CustomerName text);
SELECT CustomerName FROM ORDERS;      -- same table and column as above

-- Example 2: quoted names
CREATE TABLE "Invoices" ("InvoiceId" int, total numeric);
SELECT "InvoiceId" FROM "Invoices";   -- must match exactly

-- Gotchas / variations:
-- * The rule applies to identifiers (tables, columns, aliases, functions),
--   not to string literals, which use single quotes and keep their case.
-- * Once created with double quotes and mixed case, every later reference
--   must also be quoted with the same case.
-- * Double quotes also allow reserved words and special characters in names.
-- * Inside a quoted identifier, write a literal double quote as "".
-- * Folding is done by the parser at parse time, so the catalogs
--   (pg_class, information_schema) store the folded form.
-- * Common convention: use lowercase snake_case and avoid quoting.
pg-easy-12.title: Identifier case handling and double-quoted identifiers

pg-easy-13.syntax:
-- General form
--   'text'   single quotes -> string literal (a value)
--   "name"   double quotes -> delimited identifier (a name of a
--                table, column, alias, function, etc.)

-- Examples
SELECT 'status';            -- a constant value
SELECT "price" FROM items;  -- refers to column named price
CREATE TABLE "Order Lines" ("Qty" int);  -- allows spaces/case
SELECT "Qty" FROM "Order Lines";

-- Gotchas
-- * Unquoted identifiers are folded to lower case:
--     Qty = qty = QTY, but "Qty" <> "qty".
-- * Quoted identifiers are case-sensitive and may contain spaces
--   or reserved words, e.g. "select".
-- * To include a double quote in an identifier, double it: "a""b".
-- * To include a single quote in a string, double it: 'it''s'.
-- * An identifier is resolved against tables/columns in scope
--   during parsing; the name must be resolvable.
-- * Aliases: SELECT 1 AS "My Col"; (double quotes for output names)
-- * MySQL (in some modes) treats double quotes as strings;
--   PostgreSQL follows the SQL standard and does not.
pg-easy-13.title: Quoted identifiers vs. string literals

pg-easy-14.syntax:
-- General forms
--   character varying(n) / varchar(n)  : variable length, max n characters
--   character(n) / char(n)             : fixed length, blank-padded
--   text                               : variable length, no declared limit

CREATE TABLE city_notes (
    code   char(3),
    label  varchar(40),
    body   text
);

-- Length limit is a constraint, checked on write:
INSERT INTO city_notes (label) VALUES ('short');   -- ok
-- A value longer than n raises an error
-- (except excess trailing spaces, which are truncated;
--  an explicit cast like x::varchar(5) silently truncates)

-- Gotchas / notes
-- * varchar and text share the same underlying storage
--   representation (varlena); storage is by actual length.
-- * char(n) pads with spaces, so it can use more space;
--   padding is semantically insignificant in comparisons.
-- * varchar without n accepts any length (like text).
-- * text is not in the SQL standard, but is a Postgres native type.
-- * Long values are compressed/moved out of line (TOAST)
--   automatically, regardless of type.
-- * Use a length n only when you want the constraint itself;
--   alternatively use text with a CHECK:
ALTER TABLE city_notes
  ADD CONSTRAINT body_len CHECK (char_length(body) <= 500);
-- * Limit max is 10485760 characters for declared n.
pg-easy-14.title: Postgres character types: char(n), varchar(n), and text

pg-easy-15.syntax:
-- General form
--   column_name CHAR(n)       -- also written character(n)
--   column_name VARCHAR(n)    -- also character varying(n)
--   column_name TEXT          -- no length limit

-- Example
CREATE TABLE tags (
  code  char(6),
  label varchar(6),
  note  text
);
INSERT INTO tags VALUES ('ab', 'ab', 'ab');

-- Inspect the stored data
SELECT octet_length(code) AS code_bytes,
       octet_length(label) AS label_bytes,
       length(code) AS code_len
FROM tags;

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * n is a number of characters, not bytes.
-- * Inserting a value longer than n raises an error, unless the extra
--   characters are all spaces (then it is silently trimmed).
-- * An explicit cast, e.g. 'abcdefgh'::char(6), truncates instead of erroring.
-- * char(n) is blank-padded to n; the padding is treated as insignificant
--   when comparing two char values and is dropped when casting to other string types.
-- * length() on char(n) ignores trailing spaces; octet_length() does not.
-- * char without n means char(1); varchar without n accepts any length.
-- * In Postgres, char(n) has no speed advantage over varchar or text;
--   text/varchar are usually preferred.
pg-easy-15.title: Fixed-length vs variable-length character types

pg-easy-16.syntax:
-- Unqualified names are resolved using the search_path setting.
-- General form:
--   SHOW search_path;
--   SET search_path TO schema_a, schema_b, ...;
--   CREATE TABLE [schema.]table_name (...);

-- Example: inspect the path and see where a new table lands
SHOW search_path;                      -- lists schemas searched, in order
CREATE TABLE inventory (id int);       -- unqualified: created in the FIRST existing
                                       -- schema on the search_path
SELECT schemaname, tablename
FROM pg_tables
WHERE tablename = 'inventory';         -- shows which schema holds it

-- Example: qualify explicitly or change the path
CREATE SCHEMA staging;
CREATE TABLE staging.orders (id int);  -- explicit schema
SET search_path TO staging, public;    -- now unqualified creates go to staging

-- Gotchas:
-- * The default search_path value is "$user", <default schema>.
--   "$user" is skipped if no schema has the current user's name.
-- * System catalogs (pg_catalog) are always searched implicitly,
--   even if not listed in the path.
-- * information_schema is a standard-views schema, not a place for user tables.
-- * Lookups search in order; creation uses only the first existing schema.
-- * ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path / ALTER DATABASE ... SET makes it persistent.
-- * Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary users lack CREATE on the default schema
--   unless granted.
pg-easy-16.title: Schema name resolution and the search_path setting

pg-easy-17.title: Schema lookup configuration via the search_path setting

pg-easy-18.title: RETURNING clause in data-modifying statements

pg-easy-19.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2) VALUES (v1, v2)
  RETURNING output_expression [ [AS] output_name ] [, ...];

-- Example: return a chosen column and an expression
INSERT INTO orders (customer, qty) VALUES ('acme', 3)
  RETURNING id, qty * 2 AS double_qty;

-- Example: UPDATE and DELETE support it too
UPDATE orders SET qty = qty + 1 WHERE id = 7
  RETURNING id, qty;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE qty = 0
  RETURNING *;   -- * expands to all columns of the affected rows

-- Variations and gotchas
-- * RETURNING produces a result set, one row per affected row,
--   like a SELECT list. Aliases and expressions are allowed.
-- * Values reflect the row as stored, so defaults, serial/identity
--   values and BEFORE trigger changes are visible.
-- * For UPDATE, values are the new row; for DELETE, the removed row.
-- * Multi-row INSERT returns one row per inserted row.
-- * With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, skipped rows return nothing.
-- * Can be used in a CTE: WITH ins AS (INSERT ... RETURNING id) SELECT ...
-- * The command tag (e.g. INSERT 0 1) is separate from the result rows.
pg-easy-19.title: The RETURNING clause in data-modifying statements

pg-easy-20.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table (cols...) VALUES (...)
  ON CONFLICT [ conflict_target ] conflict_action;

-- conflict_target (optional for DO NOTHING, required for DO UPDATE):
--   (column_list)  |  ON CONSTRAINT constraint_name
-- conflict_action:
--   DO NOTHING
--   DO UPDATE SET col = expr [WHERE cond]

-- Example A: target a specific unique column
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Ann')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

-- Example B: update on conflict, using the proposed row via EXCLUDED
INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty)
VALUES ('X9', 5)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;

-- Gotchas (comments):
-- * Conflicts are detected on unique indexes / constraints (incl. primary key),
--   not on arbitrary conditions.
-- * Without a target, DO NOTHING handles any unique violation;
--   other errors (NOT NULL, CHECK, FK) still raise normally.
-- * Command tag reports only rows actually inserted (or updated).
-- * RETURNING yields only rows that were inserted/updated,
--   not rows that were skipped.
-- * In multi-row inserts, each row is judged individually.
-- * DO UPDATE cannot affect the same row twice in one statement.
pg-easy-20.title: INSERT conflict handling with ON CONFLICT

pg-easy-21.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table (cols...)
VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT [ conflict_target ] conflict_action;

-- conflict_target is one of:
--   ( col [, ...] )                 -- inference by column list
--   ( expr )                        -- index expression
--   ON CONSTRAINT constraint_name   -- name a constraint directly
--   optional WHERE predicate        -- for partial indexes

-- conflict_action is one of:
--   DO NOTHING
--   DO UPDATE SET col = expr [, ...] [WHERE cond]

-- Example 1: target a column list
CREATE TABLE users (email text UNIQUE, name text);
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Ann')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

-- Example 2: update using the proposed row via EXCLUDED
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Anna')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE
  SET name = EXCLUDED.name;

-- Gotchas
-- * For DO UPDATE the conflict target is required.
--   For DO NOTHING it may be omitted (any conflict is skipped).
-- * A column-list target must match an existing unique index or
--   unique/exclusion-compatible constraint, otherwise an error is raised.
-- * Only conflicts on the inferred index are handled by the clause;
--   a violation of a different unique constraint still raises an error.
-- * RETURNING yields only rows actually inserted or updated;
--   skipped rows are not returned.
-- * One command cannot update the same row twice via DO UPDATE.
pg-easy-21.title: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (upsert clause)

pg-easy-22.syntax:
-- Two general ways to produce an array value in SQL:
--   1) Array constructor expression:  ARRAY[elem, elem, ...]
--   2) String literal cast to an array type, using curly braces: '{elem, elem}'::type[]

-- Examples (different values from any quiz code):
SELECT ARRAY[10, 20, 30, 40];            -- integer[]
SELECT ARRAY['red', 'green'];            -- text[]
SELECT '{a,b,c}'::text[];                -- string literal with braces, cast to text[]
SELECT ARRAY[[1,2],[3,4]];               -- nested constructors give a 2-D array

-- Subquery form: ARRAY(SELECT ...) takes a query, not a value list
SELECT ARRAY(SELECT id FROM users ORDER BY id);

-- Gotchas:
-- * The constructor uses square brackets after the ARRAY keyword.
-- * String-literal form uses curly braces { }, not square brackets.
-- * Element types are inferred; mixing incompatible types raises an error.
-- * Empty array needs a type: ARRAY[]::int[]  or  '{}'::int[]
-- * Subscripts start at 1 by default: (ARRAY[5,6,7])[1] -> 5
-- * Parentheses after ARRAY are only valid around a subquery.
pg-easy-22.title: Creating array values in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-23.syntax:
-- Two ways to write an array value:
--   1) Array constructor expression:  ARRAY[elem, elem, ...]
--   2) Quoted text literal:           '{elem, elem, ...}'  (type given by cast or context)

-- Examples (different values from any quiz code):
SELECT ARRAY[10,20]::int[];          -- constructor, element type inferred from items
SELECT '{10,20}'::int[];             -- text parsed by the array type's input function
SELECT '{apple,"red pear"}'::text[]; -- quote elements containing spaces/commas/braces
SELECT '{{1,2},{3,4}}'::int[];       -- nested braces = multidimensional array
SELECT ARRAY[[1,2],[3,4]];           -- constructor for the same 2-D shape

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * A bare '{...}' is an untyped literal (type unknown) until cast or inferred from context,
--   e.g. INSERT into an int[] column or comparison with an int[] value.
-- * In the text form, NULL (unquoted, any case) is a null element; "NULL" in quotes is the string.
-- * Text form: elements are separated by commas, no SQL expressions allowed (no 1+1).
-- * ARRAY[...] accepts arbitrary expressions: ARRAY[1+1, x, f(y)].
-- * Empty array: '{}'::int[]  or  ARRAY[]::int[]  (constructor needs a cast when empty).
-- * Compare arrays with = (same dims, same elements in order); check with SELECT a = b.
-- * Default subscripts start at 1; text form can set bounds: '[0:1]={5,6}'::int[].
pg-easy-23.title: Array literals: text input form vs ARRAY constructor

pg-easy-24.syntax:
-- General form
--   array_expression[subscript]            -- single element
--   array_expression[lower:upper]          -- slice (returns array)
-- Note: a literal ARRAY[...] constructor may need parentheses
-- before subscripting in some contexts: (ARRAY[...])[n]

-- Examples
SELECT (ARRAY['a','b','c','d'])[2];     -- single element by position
SELECT (ARRAY[5,6,7,8])[2:3];           -- slice with lower:upper bounds

-- Table column example
CREATE TABLE t (tags text[]);
SELECT tags[1] FROM t;

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * By default, Postgres arrays are 1-based: the first element
--   is at subscript 1, unlike many programming languages.
-- * Array bounds can be customized when an array is created
--   from a literal like '[0:2]={x,y,z}'.
-- * Subscripting outside the array's bounds does not raise an
--   error for ordinary arrays; it yields NULL.
-- * Slices outside the bounds give an empty array, not an error.
-- * array_lower(arr, 1) and array_upper(arr, 1) report the bounds.
-- * A NULL subscript yields NULL.
pg-easy-24.title: Array subscripting and index bounds

pg-easy-25.syntax:
-- General form
array_length(anyarray, dimension int) -> int
-- dimension is 1-based: 1 = outermost axis

-- Related functions
array_ndims(arr)        -- number of dimensions
array_lower(arr, dim)   -- lower bound of a dimension (1 by default)
array_upper(arr, dim)   -- upper bound of a dimension
cardinality(arr)        -- total number of elements across all dimensions

-- Examples (different values from any quiz)
SELECT array_length(ARRAY['a','b','c','d'], 1);
SELECT array_length(ARRAY[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], 2);  -- length of the 2nd axis
SELECT array_length(ARRAY[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], 1);  -- length of the 1st axis

-- Gotchas
-- * The dimension argument must name an existing axis; for a
--   dimension the array does not have, the result is NULL.
-- * An empty array '{}' has zero dimensions, so array_length
--   on it gives NULL (not 0). cardinality('{}') gives 0.
-- * NULL array input gives NULL.
-- * Multidimensional arrays must be rectangular.
-- * array_length counts per axis; cardinality counts all elements.
pg-easy-25.title: Array dimension functions (array_length and related)

pg-easy-26.syntax:
-- General form
--   jsonb_expr -> 'key'      -- object field by key
--   jsonb_expr -> int        -- array element by 0-based index (negative counts from end)
--   jsonb_expr ->> 'key'     -- same lookup, result converted to text
--   jsonb_expr #> '{a,b}'    -- path lookup (jsonb);  #>> returns text

-- Example setup: col `doc` is jsonb = {"shop": {"city": "Oslo", "tags": ["a","b"]}}
SELECT doc -> 'shop'              FROM t;  -- lookup one level
SELECT doc -> 'shop' -> 'city'    FROM t;  -- operators chain left to right
SELECT doc -> 'shop' -> 'tags' -> 0 FROM t;  -- array index
SELECT doc #>> '{shop,city}'      FROM t;  -- path form, text result

-- Gotchas
-- * The result type of -> is jsonb (or json for json columns); ->> is text.
-- * Text key on an object, integer on an array; a mismatch yields NULL.
-- * A missing key or index yields NULL, not an error.
-- * Chaining after ->> fails: text has no -> operator.
-- * Comparing to a string: use ->> 'k' = 'x', or -> 'k' = '"x"'::jsonb.
-- * Operator precedence: parenthesize, e.g. (doc -> 'k') IS NULL.
pg-easy-26.title: jsonb accessor operators (-> and ->>)

pg-easy-27.syntax:
-- General form
--   jsonb_expr  <operator>  key_or_index
-- Operators that extract a single element:
--   ->   extract an object field by key, or an array element by integer index
--   ->>  same lookup, but with a different result type than ->
-- Path variants (take a text[] path):
--   #>   and   #>>

-- Example table: orders(info jsonb)
-- info = '{"customer": {"city": "Oslo"}, "tags": ["a","b"], "qty": 3}'

SELECT info -> 'customer'              FROM orders;  -- lookup by key
SELECT info -> 'tags' -> 0             FROM orders;  -- chain operators; integer = array index
SELECT info #> '{customer,city}'       FROM orders;  -- path lookup

-- Check the result type with pg_typeof():
SELECT pg_typeof(info -> 'qty'), pg_typeof(info ->> 'qty') FROM orders;

-- Gotchas
-- * Missing key or out-of-range index yields SQL NULL for both operators.
-- * A JSON null value is different from SQL NULL when the result stays jsonb.
-- * Operators can be chained, but the left side must be jsonb (or json).
-- * Casting is needed for numeric comparisons on extracted values:
--     WHERE (info ->> 'qty')::int > 2
-- * Use the result type to decide which operator can be chained further.
-- * Negative integer index counts from the end of an array: info -> 'tags' -> -1
pg-easy-27.title: jsonb field access operators

pg-easy-29.syntax:
-- General form (variadic, arguments alternate key, value, key, value, ...)
jsonb_build_object(key1, value1, key2, value2, ...)  -- returns jsonb object
jsonb_build_array(value1, value2, ...)               -- returns jsonb array

-- Examples
SELECT jsonb_build_object('name', 'Ada', 'age', 36, 'admin', false);
SELECT jsonb_build_array('x', 2, NULL, true);

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Arguments are taken in pairs; an odd number of arguments raises an error.
-- * Keys are converted to text; a key cannot be NULL.
-- * Each value keeps its SQL type when converted to JSON:
--     numbers become JSON numbers, booleans become JSON booleans,
--     text becomes JSON strings, NULL becomes JSON null.
-- * Values may be of mixed types (the function accepts "any" arguments).
-- * Values can be nested: another jsonb_build_object(...) or an array.
-- * Untyped literals like 'abc' are treated as text.
-- * json_build_object is the json (not jsonb) variant; jsonb sorts keys
--   and removes duplicate keys (last value wins).
-- * Empty call: jsonb_build_object() returns {}.
pg-easy-29.title: Building JSON with jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array

pg-easy-30.syntax:
-- General idea: Postgres has several "current time" functions.
-- Each one differs in WHEN the value is taken.
--
--   transaction_timestamp()  / CURRENT_TIMESTAMP -> start of the current transaction
--   statement_timestamp()                        -> start of the current statement
--   clock_timestamp()                            -> actual time at each call
--   now()                                        -> traditional name for transaction_timestamp()
--   timeofday()                                  -> like clock_timestamp(), returns text

-- Example: compare the functions across statements
BEGIN;
SELECT statement_timestamp() AS stmt, clock_timestamp() AS wall;
SELECT pg_sleep(2);
SELECT statement_timestamp() AS stmt, clock_timestamp() AS wall;
COMMIT;

-- Example: several calls inside a single statement
SELECT clock_timestamp() AS c1, pg_sleep(1), clock_timestamp() AS c2;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Compare each function's definition to know whether it changes
--   between statements, or between calls within one statement.
-- * A new transaction gets a fresh value; autocommit means each
--   statement is its own transaction.
-- * Column DEFAULT now() is evaluated at insert time, per transaction.
-- * CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(0) rounds to a given fractional-second precision.
-- * Use clock_timestamp() for timing code durations.
pg-easy-30.title: Date/time functions and when their values are fixed

pg-easy-31.syntax:
-- General forms (no parentheses for the SQL-standard keywords):
--   CURRENT_DATE
--   CURRENT_TIME        [(precision)]
--   CURRENT_TIMESTAMP   [(precision)]
--   LOCALTIME / LOCALTIMESTAMP [(precision)]
--   now()               -- Postgres function, same as transaction start time
--   clock_timestamp()   -- actual wall-clock time, changes within a statement

-- Inspect types with pg_typeof():
SELECT pg_typeof(CURRENT_TIME)      AS t1,
       pg_typeof(LOCALTIMESTAMP)    AS t2,
       pg_typeof(clock_timestamp()) AS t3;

-- Example: rows created in the last 7 days
SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - interval '7 days';

-- Gotchas (as comments):
-- * CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, now() are fixed
--   at the start of the transaction, not each statement.
-- * LOCALTIME/LOCALTIMESTAMP return types WITHOUT time zone;
--   CURRENT_TIME/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP return types WITH time zone.
-- * CURRENT_DATE written as CURRENT_DATE() is a syntax error.
-- * Comparing a date to a timestamptz casts the date to midnight
--   in the session TimeZone.
-- * Cast explicitly when needed: now()::date, ts::timestamp
pg-easy-31.title: Current date/time functions and their return types

pg-easy-32.syntax:
-- General forms (no-argument, return timestamptz unless noted)
--   now()                  -- start of current transaction
--   transaction_timestamp()-- same value as now()
--   statement_timestamp()  -- start of current statement
--   clock_timestamp()      -- actual wall-clock time at the moment of the call
--   CURRENT_TIMESTAMP      -- SQL-standard, no parentheses; transaction start
--   CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME  -- transaction start, as date / timetz

-- Example: compare sources inside one transaction
BEGIN;
SELECT transaction_timestamp() AS tx_start,
       statement_timestamp()   AS stmt_start,
       clock_timestamp()       AS wall_clock;
SELECT pg_sleep(0.5);
SELECT transaction_timestamp() AS tx_start,
       statement_timestamp()   AS stmt_start,
       clock_timestamp()       AS wall_clock;
COMMIT;

-- Example: measuring elapsed time of a step
SELECT clock_timestamp() AS t0 \gset
SELECT clock_timestamp() - :'t0'::timestamptz AS elapsed;

-- Gotchas
-- * Each function has its own "when is it frozen?" rule; check which
--   moment it reports before relying on it.
-- * Within a single row-producing query, volatile functions can be
--   evaluated per row; stable ones are evaluated consistently.
-- * timeofday() is a legacy text-returning variant of the wall clock.
-- * Use a stable source for created_at defaults that must agree
--   across a transaction; use a changing source for profiling.
pg-easy-32.title: Date/time current-value functions and their time sources

pg-easy-33.syntax:
-- General form:
-- COALESCE(value1, value2, ..., valueN)
-- Evaluates arguments left to right and yields the first
-- argument that is not NULL. If all are NULL, yields NULL.

-- Example 1: fallback to a literal
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, 'anonymous') FROM users;

-- Example 2: chain of fallbacks
SELECT COALESCE(mobile_phone, home_phone, work_phone, 'none') AS contact
FROM people;

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * Later arguments are only evaluated if needed (short-circuit).
-- * All arguments must resolve to a compatible common type,
--   otherwise Postgres raises a type error.
-- * Only NULL triggers the fallback; empty strings and 0
--   are real values and are returned as-is.
-- * If every argument is NULL the result is NULL, so end the
--   list with a non-null literal when you need a guaranteed value.
-- * Useful in aggregates: COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) for empty groups.
-- * Related: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b.
pg-easy-33.title: COALESCE for handling missing values

pg-easy-34.syntax:
-- General form
COALESCE(value1, value2, ..., valueN)

-- Arguments are evaluated left to right; the result is the
-- first argument that is not NULL. If every argument is NULL,
-- the result is NULL.

-- Example 1: fallback for an optional column
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'guest') AS display_name
FROM users;

-- Example 2: replace NULL in an aggregate
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Later arguments are only evaluated if needed (short-circuit),
--   so COALESCE(x, 1/0) will not error when x is not NULL.
-- * All arguments must resolve to a common data type, or Postgres
--   raises a type error.
-- * An empty string '' is NOT NULL, so COALESCE does not skip it.
--   Use COALESCE(NULLIF(col, ''), 'default') to treat '' as missing.
-- * Equivalent to CASE WHEN v1 IS NOT NULL THEN v1 ... END.
-- * COALESCE is standard SQL; NVL / IFNULL are not Postgres functions.
pg-easy-34.title: COALESCE conditional expression

pg-easy-35.syntax:
-- General form
SELECT DISTINCT ON (expr [, ...]) select_list
FROM table
ORDER BY expr [, ...];

-- Plain DISTINCT: removes duplicate rows by comparing ALL selected columns
SELECT DISTINCT city, country FROM venues;

-- DISTINCT ON: for each group of rows sharing the ON expression(s),
-- only the FIRST row of the group is kept. "First" is defined by ORDER BY.
-- Other columns in the select list may differ and are kept from that row.

-- Example: latest reading per sensor
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sensor_id) sensor_id, reading, taken_at
FROM readings
ORDER BY sensor_id, taken_at DESC;

-- Example: cheapest product per category, with all columns
SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) *
FROM products
ORDER BY category, price ASC;

-- Gotchas
-- * The ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions.
-- * Without ORDER BY, which row is kept is unpredictable.
-- * NULLs are treated as equal to each other (one group).
-- * DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL extension, not standard SQL.
-- * Add tie-breaker columns to ORDER BY for deterministic results.
-- * It is applied after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING, before LIMIT.
pg-easy-35.title: DISTINCT ON in SELECT

pg-easy-36.syntax:
-- General form
SELECT DISTINCT ON (expr [, ...]) select_list
FROM table
[ORDER BY expr [ASC|DESC] [, ...]];

-- Keeps only the first row of each set of rows that share the same DISTINCT ON expressions.
-- "First" is defined solely by the ORDER BY clause.

-- Example: latest reading per sensor
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sensor_id) sensor_id, reading, taken_at
FROM readings
ORDER BY sensor_id, taken_at DESC;

-- Example: cheapest product per category
SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY category, price ASC, name;

-- Gotchas:
-- * Without ORDER BY, the row kept per group is unspecified.
-- * The DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY
--   expressions (otherwise an error is raised).
-- * Ordering by the group column alone only groups the rows; it does not
--   decide which row inside each group is first.
-- * Add extra ORDER BY columns after the group columns to choose the row.
--   Add a unique tie-breaker column for fully repeatable results.
-- * NULLs are treated as equal to each other for grouping.
-- * DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL extension, not standard SQL.
-- * Applied after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and window functions, before LIMIT.
pg-easy-36.title: SELECT DISTINCT ON row selection

docs.title: PostgreSQL Docs: Value Storage Type Conversion

pg-easy-37.title: Boolean literals and assignment conversion

docs.title: Lexical Structure: Identifiers and Key Words

pg-easy-38.syntax:
-- Boolean constants (SQL key words):
--   TRUE | FALSE | NULL (unknown)
-- Also accepted as string literals cast to boolean:
--   'true','t','yes','y','on','1'  /  'false','f','no','n','off','0'
--   (leading/trailing whitespace ignored; string input is case-insensitive)

-- Examples
SELECT TRUE AS a, false AS b;
SELECT 'Yes'::boolean;
CREATE TABLE flags (id int, active boolean DEFAULT true);
INSERT INTO flags VALUES (1, 'on'), (2, FALSE);
SELECT * FROM flags WHERE active IS TRUE;

-- Key words and unquoted identifiers: PostgreSQL folds them
-- to a single case when parsing (lower case for identifiers),
-- so SELECT, select, SeLeCt are the same.
-- Quoted identifiers ("Name") ARE case-sensitive.
-- String literal contents are NOT folded, but boolean input
-- parsing of strings ignores case.

-- Gotchas
--   Output is displayed as t / f in psql.
--   Use IS TRUE / IS NOT TRUE / IS UNKNOWN to handle NULL.
--   Numbers other than '1'/'0' strings are not valid boolean strings.
pg-easy-38.title: Boolean literals and keyword case rules in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-39.syntax:
-- Column constraint:
--   column_name type CHECK (boolean_expression)
-- Table constraint (may reference several columns):
--   [CONSTRAINT name] CHECK (boolean_expression)

CREATE TABLE members (
  age      INTEGER CONSTRAINT age_adult CHECK (age >= 18),
  min_qty  INTEGER,
  max_qty  INTEGER,
  CONSTRAINT qty_order CHECK (min_qty <= max_qty)
);

-- Add to an existing table:
ALTER TABLE members
  ADD CONSTRAINT age_cap CHECK (age < 150);

-- Add without scanning existing rows, validate later:
ALTER TABLE members
  ADD CONSTRAINT age_cap2 CHECK (age < 150) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE members VALIDATE CONSTRAINT age_cap2;

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * The expression must evaluate to boolean.
-- * A row is rejected only if the result is FALSE;
--   TRUE and NULL both pass. Add NOT NULL to forbid NULLs.
-- * Violations raise an error (SQLSTATE 23514) and the
--   statement fails.
-- * Only the row's own columns may be used; no subqueries
--   to other tables. Expression should be immutable.
-- * Auto-generated name looks like table_column_check.
-- * Drop with: ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT name;
pg-easy-39.title: CHECK constraints in table definitions

pg-easy-40.title: Inspecting query plans with EXPLAIN options

pg-easy-41.syntax:
-- Postgres exposes metadata in two places:
--   1) pg_catalog.*         : native system catalogs and views (Postgres-specific)
--   2) information_schema.* : views defined by the SQL standard (ISO/IEC 9075)
--
-- General form:
--   SELECT ... FROM <schema>.<view> WHERE ...;

-- Example: list tables via the standard schema
SELECT table_name, table_type
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public';

-- Example: the Postgres-native equivalent
SELECT schemaname, tablename
FROM pg_catalog.pg_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'public';

-- Notes and gotchas:
-- * information_schema views use standard names (table_name, column_name,
--   data_type, is_nullable) and exist in other databases such as MySQL
--   and SQL Server, though coverage varies.
-- * pg_catalog objects usually start with pg_ (pg_class, pg_index,
--   pg_stat_*). They expose Postgres-only details: OIDs, access methods,
--   runtime statistics, and so on.
-- * pg_catalog is always on the search path, so the prefix is optional.
-- * information_schema shows only objects the current user owns or has
--   privileges on; pg_catalog generally shows everything.
-- * information_schema is usually slower and less detailed than pg_catalog.
-- * Prefix check: a view named pg_* is Postgres-specific by convention.
pg-easy-41.title: System catalogs vs. information_schema

pg-easy-42.syntax:
-- General forms
-- Postgres system catalog view:
SELECT schemaname, tablename, tableowner FROM pg_catalog.pg_views_example;  -- placeholder shape only
-- Standard-defined view:
SELECT table_schema, table_name, table_type FROM information_schema.tables;

-- Example 1: Postgres catalog view, one schema
SELECT schemaname, tablename, tableowner, tablespace
FROM pg_catalog.pg_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'sales';

-- Example 2: standard view, one schema
SELECT table_name, table_type
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'sales';

-- Notes / gotchas
-- * Both views only describe the database you are connected to.
--   Cross-database listing needs separate connections (or pg_database for the database names themselves).
-- * information_schema follows the SQL standard: portable column names (table_schema, table_name, table_type),
--   and it also lists views (table_type = 'VIEW' or 'BASE TABLE').
-- * information_schema only shows objects the current role owns or has some privilege on.
-- * pg_catalog views expose Postgres-specific columns; check the docs for the exact column list
--   of pg_tables (e.g. tablespace, indexes/trigger/rule flags).
-- * pg_tables lists only tables (not views); pg_views, pg_matviews, pg_indexes cover other kinds.
-- * Neither view gives row counts or sizes. Use pg_class.reltuples (estimate),
--   count(*), or pg_relation_size() / pg_total_relation_size().
-- * psql shortcut: \dt  (tables), \dt sales.*
pg-easy-42.title: Listing tables: system catalogs vs information_schema

pg-easy-43.syntax:
-- General form (run inside psql, not SQL):
--   \d[S+] [pattern]     describe objects; pattern is optional, supports * and ?
--   S  = include system objects
--   +  = show extra detail (size, description, etc.)

-- Examples:
\d orders          -- columns, indexes, constraints of one relation
\dt sales.*        -- tables in the sales schema only
\dt+ *.audit_*     -- tables matching a name pattern, with sizes

-- Each letter after \d selects an object kind. Common ones:
--   \dt  tables         \dv  views
--   \di  indexes        \ds  sequences
--   \df  functions      \dT  data types
--   \du  roles          \dx  extensions
--   \l   databases      \dm  materialized views
--   \dn  and \dN etc. exist for other catalog object kinds
--   \dp  access privileges

-- Gotchas:
-- * Meta-commands are psql features, not SQL; no semicolon needed.
-- * Without S, system objects are hidden by default.
-- * Patterns are case-folded unless double-quoted.
-- * Plain \d lists tables, views, sequences, etc. together.
-- * Use \? inside psql to list all backslash commands.
-- * Equivalent SQL: query the pg_catalog or information_schema views.
pg-easy-43.title: psql describe meta-commands (\d family)

pg-easy-44.syntax:
-- General form (run inside psql, not as SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S+] [pattern]
-- The letter after \d picks the kind of object to list.
-- pattern is optional; it supports * and ? wildcards and schema.name.
-- S  = include system objects, + = add extra detail (size, description, etc.)

-- Examples:
\dt public.*        -- tables in schema public
\di+ idx_*          -- indexes starting with idx_, with extra detail
\ds                 -- sequences

-- Common letters in the family:
--   \d   relations (tables, views, sequences); \d name describes one object
--   \dt  tables         \di  indexes
--   \dv  views          \dm  materialized views
--   \ds  sequences      \dT  data types
--   \dn  schemas        \dx  extensions
--   \du / \dg  roles    \l   databases (not a \d form)
--   \dp  access privileges
--   \dF  text search configs
-- Related: functions, aggregates, and procedures each have their own
--   \d-letter; see the docs list under \d[S+] variants.

-- Gotchas:
--   Letters are case-sensitive (\dt vs \dT are different).
--   System objects are hidden unless S is added (e.g. \dfS).
--   Without a pattern, only objects visible in the search_path are listed;
--   use \dt *.* to see all schemas.
--   \set ECHO_HIDDEN on shows the SQL psql runs behind each command.
pg-easy-44.title: psql describe meta-commands (\d family)

pg-easy-45.syntax:
-- General form (psql meta-command, not SQL; typed at the psql prompt)
--   \timing [on|off]
--
-- Example session:
--   \timing on
--   SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
--   -- result table, then a line like: Time: 1.234 ms
--
--   \timing off
--   -- no more timing lines are printed
--
-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * \timing with no argument toggles the current state.
-- * \timing on/off sets it explicitly.
-- * It is a client-side measurement made by psql: it includes
--   network round trip and result transfer, not only server work.
-- * Time is reported in milliseconds; long times also show
--   a h:mm:ss.fff breakdown.
-- * Applies to every statement sent afterwards in the session,
--   including ones run with \g or from \i files.
-- * Can be enabled at startup via ~/.psqlrc.
-- * For server-side execution time use:
--   EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 7;
-- * psql -c / -f scripts: \timing also works inside -f files.
pg-easy-45.title: psql meta-commands for query execution statistics

pg-easy-46.syntax:
-- General form: functions that take no arguments report session state
-- SELECT <function>();   -- some are also usable without parentheses (e.g. current_user)

-- Examples
SELECT current_user;            -- role the session is running as
SELECT session_user;            -- role that opened the session
SELECT current_schema();        -- first existing schema on search_path
SELECT current_schemas(false);  -- array of schemas searched, excluding implicit ones
SELECT inet_server_port();      -- server port of the connection
SELECT version();               -- server version string

-- Gotchas
-- * Return values describe the current session/connection, not server-wide config.
-- * Many return type name (identifier) or text; names are not the same as OIDs.
-- * OIDs are numeric identifiers in system catalogs (e.g. pg_database.oid),
--   and are looked up there rather than returned by most session functions.
-- * Values may differ between sessions, e.g. after SET ROLE or SET search_path.
-- * Settings in postgresql.conf are read with SHOW or current_setting('name').
-- * pg_database lists all databases in the cluster: SELECT datname, oid FROM pg_database;
pg-easy-46.title: Session information functions

pg-easy-47.syntax:
-- General form: functions that report who a session is
--   SELECT session_user, current_user, user, current_role;
--   SET ROLE role_name;      -- change the active role for the session
--   RESET ROLE;              -- go back to the session's initial role
--   SET LOCAL ROLE role_name; -- only until end of current transaction
--
-- Example (hypothetical roles: login role 'dana', member of 'reporting')
--   -- connected as dana
--   SET ROLE reporting;
--   SELECT session_user, current_user;
--   RESET ROLE;
--
-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * session_user = role identified at connection time (authentication).
-- * current_user = the user identity used for permission checks now;
--   it is what privilege checks and default ownership use.
-- * current_role is a synonym for current_user; user is too.
-- * These are SQL keywords: write them without parentheses.
-- * Inside a SECURITY DEFINER function, current_user is the
--   function owner, while session_user is unchanged.
-- * SET ROLE only works to roles the session user is a member of
--   (or a superuser may pick any role).
-- * The OS user running the server is a separate concept
--   and is not reported by these.
-- * The database owner is shown via pg_database.datdba,
--   not by these functions.
-- * Also see: SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION to change session_user
--   (superuser only, in most cases).
pg-easy-47.title: Session identity functions and role switching

pg-easy-48.syntax:
-- General forms (system information functions and settings)
SELECT <function_or_setting>;
SHOW <parameter>;
SELECT current_setting('<parameter>');

-- Examples of related version-inspection tools
SHOW server_version;                    -- version number text only, e.g. 16.3
SELECT current_setting('server_version_num');  -- integer-style version as text
SELECT current_database(), current_user;       -- other session info functions

-- psql client side (not SQL, run at the psql prompt or shell):
--   \conninfo          -- describes the current connection
--   psql --version     -- prints the client program's version (shell)

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * Server-side functions run on the server, so they describe the server,
--   not the psql program you typed into.
-- * Some functions return descriptive text, others return a bare number;
--   check the return type with pg_typeof(...), e.g.
--     SELECT pg_typeof(current_setting('server_version_num'));
-- * current_setting() returns text, so cast it when comparing numerically:
--     SELECT current_setting('server_version_num')::int >= 140000;
-- * Application code should prefer the numeric setting for version checks
--   rather than parsing descriptive text.
-- * Migration tools keep their own schema version tables; Postgres itself
--   has no built-in notion of an application schema version.
pg-easy-48.title: Inspecting server and client version information

pg-easy-49.syntax:
-- General form: how a client picks the server endpoint
--   postgresql://user@host:PORT/dbname
--   psql -h HOST -p PORT -U USER -d DBNAME

-- Server side (postgresql.conf):
--   port = <integer>              -- TCP port the server listens on
--   listen_addresses = 'localhost' -- which interfaces to bind
--   unix_socket_directories = '/var/run/postgresql'

-- Example: connecting to a server configured for a custom port
--   psql -h db.example.com -p 6543 -U app -d shop
--   postgresql://app@db.example.com:6543/shop

-- Inspect the running server's setting from SQL:
SHOW port;
SELECT name, setting, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'port';

-- Gotchas:
-- * If -p / the URL port / PGPORT is omitted, the client uses its compiled-in
--   default (the same default the server ships with).
-- * Changing port requires a server restart, not just a reload.
-- * The port also names the Unix socket file (.s.PGSQL.<port>).
-- * Several clusters on one host each need a distinct port.
-- * Other database products use their own, different default ports;
--   do not assume one product's port applies to another.
-- * Env var PGPORT sets the client's default port.
pg-easy-49.title: Server connection settings: port and listen addresses

pg-easy-51.syntax:
-- General forms
--   CAST(expression AS target_type)   -- SQL standard
--   expression::target_type           -- PostgreSQL-specific shorthand
--   target_type 'literal'             -- typed literal, e.g. date '2024-01-31'
--   typename(expression)              -- function-style, only for some type names

-- Examples
SELECT CAST('42.5' AS numeric);
SELECT '2024-03-01'::date;
SELECT CAST(7.9 AS integer);      -- numeric to integer conversion

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * Both forms invoke the same cast mechanism (explicit cast);
--   they differ in syntax, portability and operator precedence.
-- * :: binds very tightly: -2::text applies to 2 first.
--   Use parentheses: (a + b)::int, or CAST(a + b AS int).
-- * Invalid input raises an error, e.g. 'abc'::integer
--   -> invalid input syntax for type integer.
-- * Casting to varchar(n) / char(n) truncates explicitly cast values.
-- * Whitespace in input strings is usually tolerated by numeric types.
-- * Array types: CAST('{1,2}' AS int[]) or '{1,2}'::int[].
-- * Casts can be defined with CREATE CAST; explicit casts may be
--   allowed where implicit/assignment ones are not.
pg-easy-51.title: Type conversion: CAST vs :: and related forms

pg-easy-53.syntax:
-- General form
--   <timestamp expr> {+ | -} INTERVAL '<quantity> <unit>'  -> same kind of timestamp
--   <date> + <integer>                                     -> date (days)
--   <timestamp> - <timestamp>                              -> interval

-- Examples
SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '3 hours';
SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-01-31 10:00' + INTERVAL '1 month';
SELECT DATE '2024-03-01' + 10;                  -- date + integer = date
SELECT DATE '2024-03-01' + INTERVAL '10 days';  -- date + interval = timestamp

-- Current-time functions (differ in when they are evaluated):
--   now(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, transaction_timestamp()
--       fixed at the start of the transaction
--   statement_timestamp()   start of the current statement
--   clock_timestamp()       actual wall-clock time, changes during a statement
--   timeofday()             wall-clock time, returned as text

-- Gotchas
--   Result type follows the left operand and the interval:
--     timestamptz + interval -> timestamptz
--     date + interval        -> timestamp (time part 00:00:00)
--   Month/day arithmetic is calendar-based: '1 month' added to Jan 31
--   gives the last day of February, and '1 day' is not always 24 hours
--   across DST changes for timestamptz.
--   Units: microseconds, milliseconds, second, minute, hour, day,
--   week, month, year, decade, century, millennium.
--   Cast with ::date to drop the time: (now() + INTERVAL '2 days')::date
pg-easy-53.title: Date/time arithmetic with intervals and current-time functions

docs.title: Date/Time Types: interval input and output

pg-easy-54.syntax:
-- General forms
-- AGE(timestamp, timestamp)  -> interval   (first minus second)
-- AGE(timestamp)             -> interval   (current_date at midnight minus the argument)

-- Examples (different values from any quiz)
SELECT AGE(timestamp '2020-06-15', timestamp '2020-03-10');
SELECT AGE(timestamp '2019-01-31', timestamp '2021-04-02');

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * The result is an interval, not an integer.
-- * It is "symbolic": the result is broken into years, months and days
--   (and time fields), not a single total number of days.
-- * Subtraction is done field by field, borrowing from months as needed,
--   so it differs from plain subtraction:
--     timestamp - timestamp   -> interval expressed mostly in days
--     date - date             -> integer number of days
-- * If the first argument is earlier than the second, the result is negative.
-- * Use EXTRACT(year FROM AGE(...)) to pull out a single field.
-- * Works with timestamp, timestamptz and date (dates are cast to timestamp).
-- * Compare with: SELECT timestamp '2020-06-15' - timestamp '2020-03-10';
pg-easy-54.title: AGE function for date and timestamp differences

docs.title: Table Functions in the FROM clause

pg-easy-55.syntax:
-- General form
-- generate_series(start, stop [, step])
-- A set-returning function: used in FROM, it behaves like a table
-- and can yield many rows, each with one value in a column.

-- Example 1: integers with a step
SELECT * FROM generate_series(10, 30, 10);

-- Example 2: timestamps (step is an interval, required for dates)
SELECT d::date
FROM generate_series(
  '2024-01-01'::timestamp,
  '2024-01-03'::timestamp,
  interval '1 day'
) AS d;

-- Variations and gotchas
-- * Supported types: integer, bigint, numeric, timestamp, timestamptz.
-- * Negative step counts down: generate_series(9, 3, -3)
-- * Step of 0 raises an error.
-- * If start > stop with a positive step, zero rows are returned.
-- * Both endpoints are inclusive when the step lands on them.
-- * Name the column: SELECT n FROM generate_series(1, 4) AS t(n);
-- * Handy for building test data, calendars, and filling gaps
--   via LEFT JOIN.
-- * In the SELECT list it also expands into rows:
--   SELECT generate_series(1, 3);
pg-easy-55.title: Set-returning function: generate_series

pg-easy-56.syntax:
-- General form
-- agg_func(expression, delimiter [ORDER BY sort_expr]) ... FROM table [GROUP BY col]
--
-- string_agg(value, delimiter)
--   value and delimiter must be text (or bytea for both)
--   NULL values are skipped; delimiter is not added for them
--   returns NULL if there are no non-NULL input values
--   the delimiter is placed only between values, not at the ends

-- Example 1: one string per group
SELECT dept, string_agg(emp_name, '; ') AS members
FROM staff
GROUP BY dept;

-- Example 2: ordering inside the aggregate
SELECT string_agg(city, ' | ' ORDER BY city DESC)
FROM offices;

-- Gotchas
-- * Without ORDER BY inside the call, the order of joined values is
--   unspecified and depends on the scan order.
-- * Result is a single text value per group, not an array
--   (compare array_agg(x), which returns an array type).
-- * Non-text columns need a cast: string_agg(id::text, ',')
-- * DISTINCT is allowed: string_agg(DISTINCT col, ',')
--   (then ORDER BY must match the aggregated expression)
-- * Not the same as string_to_table / regexp_split_to_table,
--   which split a string into rows.
pg-easy-56.title: Aggregate functions with a delimiter argument

pg-easy-57.syntax:
-- General form:
-- regexp_replace(source, pattern, replacement [, flags])
-- regexp_replace(source, pattern, replacement, start [, N [, flags]])  -- PG 15+

-- Examples (different inputs):
SELECT regexp_replace('a.b.c.d', '\.', ':');        -- one replacement, see flags below
SELECT regexp_replace('a.b.c.d', '\.', ':', 'g');   -- flag changes scope
SELECT regexp_replace('Hello World', 'o', '0', 'gi');
SELECT regexp_replace('John Smith', '(\w+) (\w+)', '\2, \1');  -- backrefs \1..\9

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * Pattern is a POSIX regular expression, not a literal string.
-- * Without flags, only the FIRST match is replaced.
-- * 'g' = replace all matches (global); 'i' = case-insensitive;
--   flags can be combined, e.g. 'gi'.
-- * Replacement: \1-\9 insert captured groups, \& inserts whole match;
--   write \\ for a literal backslash.
-- * If there is no match, the source string is returned unchanged.
-- * Result is text. Input is not modified.
-- * For plain literal replacement of all occurrences, replace(src, from, to)
--   is simpler and does not use regex.
-- * Invalid regex or unknown flag raises an error.
pg-easy-57.title: regexp_replace pattern substitution and flags

pg-easy-58.syntax:
-- General form:
--   text_expr  OPERATOR  pattern
-- Operators:
--   ~     matches regex, case-sensitive
--   ~*    matches regex, case-insensitive
--   !~    does not match regex, case-sensitive
--   !~*   does not match regex, case-insensitive

-- Examples (different data from any quiz):
SELECT * FROM products WHERE sku ~ '^AB[0-9]+$';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email ~* '@example\.com$';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE city !~ 'ville';

-- Gotchas:
-- * Unlike LIKE, a regex is NOT anchored: it matches anywhere
--   in the string unless you use ^ (start) or $ (end).
-- * Regex special characters (. * + ? | ( ) [ ] \) need escaping
--   to be literal, e.g. '\.'.
-- * LIKE uses % and _ ; regex uses .* and . instead.
-- * Related: SIMILAR TO, and ILIKE for case-insensitive LIKE.
-- * Functions: regexp_match(), regexp_replace(), substring(s FROM pattern).
-- * NULL input gives NULL, which WHERE treats as not true.
pg-easy-58.title: POSIX regular expression match operators

pg-easy-60.syntax:
-- General form
--   expr1 IS DISTINCT FROM expr2
--   expr1 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM expr2

-- Example: finding changed rows
SELECT id
FROM prices
WHERE new_price IS DISTINCT FROM old_price;

-- Example: null-safe join condition
SELECT *
FROM t1 JOIN t2
  ON t1.code IS NOT DISTINCT FROM t2.code;

-- Background: ordinary comparison operators (=, <>, <, >)
--   follow three-valued logic. If either operand is NULL,
--   the result is NULL (unknown), not true or false.
--   WHERE and JOIN ON keep a row only when the condition is true.
--
-- IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe counterpart of <> and =:
--   * two NULLs are considered equal (not distinct)
--   * a NULL and a non-NULL value are considered different
--   * two non-NULL values are compared as with = / <>
--   * the result is always true or false, never NULL
--
-- Related forms:
--   expr IS NULL / IS NOT NULL      -- test a single value
--   row1 IS DISTINCT FROM row2      -- works on row constructors too
--
-- Gotchas:
--   * NULL = NULL yields NULL, not true
--   * NOT (a = b) is not the same as a IS DISTINCT FROM b when NULLs are present
--   * Index usage on the operator can differ from plain =; check with EXPLAIN
--   * Operand types must be comparable, as with =
pg-easy-60.title: Null-aware comparison operators in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-61.title: Enumerated types in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-63.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE DOMAIN name [AS] data_type
    [ COLLATE collation ]
    [ DEFAULT expression ]
    [ NOT NULL | NULL ]
    [ CONSTRAINT cname CHECK (expression) ... ];
-- VALUE in CHECK stands for the value being tested

-- Example 1: a domain for short codes
CREATE DOMAIN zip_code AS text
    DEFAULT '00000'
    CONSTRAINT zip_format CHECK (VALUE ~ '^[0-9]{5}$');

CREATE TABLE shops (
    id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    zip  zip_code NOT NULL
);

-- Example 2: change a domain later
ALTER DOMAIN zip_code ADD CONSTRAINT not_zero CHECK (VALUE <> '00000');
ALTER DOMAIN zip_code DROP CONSTRAINT not_zero;
DROP DOMAIN zip_code;  -- fails if columns still use it (add CASCADE to drop them too)

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * A domain is a distinct type built on a base type, with optional
--   default, NOT NULL and CHECK rules attached.
-- * It can be used for columns, function parameters, casts, variables.
-- * Values of a domain are usable with operators of the base type.
-- * CHECK passes when the expression is TRUE or NULL (NULL is allowed
--   unless you add NOT NULL).
-- * ALTER DOMAIN ADD CONSTRAINT validates existing data in columns using it
--   (use NOT VALID to skip, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT).
-- * Domain constraints are checked when a value is converted to the domain,
--   e.g. on insert/update or an explicit cast: CAST(x AS zip_code).
pg-easy-63.title: User-defined types with constraints (CREATE DOMAIN)

pg-easy-64.syntax:
-- Server-side form (SQL command):
COPY table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)];
COPY table_name | (query) TO 'path' | PROGRAM 'cmd' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)];

-- Client-side form (psql meta-command, one line, no trailing semicolon needed):
\copy table_name [(col, ...)] FROM 'path' | STDIN [WITH (option, ...)]
\copy (query) TO 'path' | STDOUT [WITH (option, ...)]

-- Examples:
COPY invoices TO '/var/lib/postgresql/out/invoices.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER);
\copy invoices FROM 'invoices_in.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER)

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * COPY with a file name: the file is read/written by the server process,
--   path resolved on the server's filesystem, using the server OS account's permissions.
-- * COPY with a file needs superuser or membership in pg_read_server_files /
--   pg_write_server_files; PROGRAM needs pg_execute_server_program.
-- * \copy: psql opens the file itself as the client user, then streams the data
--   to the server via COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT. Path is relative to psql's
--   working directory.
-- * COPY ... FROM STDIN / TO STDOUT transfers data over the connection (used by drivers).
-- * Options: FORMAT text|csv|binary, DELIMITER, NULL, HEADER, QUOTE, ESCAPE.
-- * COPY is not a normal INSERT: it is fast, and triggers fire but rules do not.
-- * Whole load fails if any row is bad (unless ON_ERROR is set in newer versions).
pg-easy-64.title: Bulk loading and exporting with COPY and psql's \copy

pg-easy-65.syntax:
-- General form
COPY table_name [ (col1, col2, ...) ]
    FROM { 'filename' | STDIN | PROGRAM 'cmd' }
    [ WITH ( option [, ...] ) ];

COPY { table_name [ (cols) ] | (query) }
    TO { 'filename' | STDOUT | PROGRAM 'cmd' }
    [ WITH ( option [, ...] ) ];

-- Example: load a CSV file (server-side path)
COPY invoices (id, customer, total)
    FROM '/data/invoices.csv'
    WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);

-- Example: export a query result
COPY (SELECT id, total FROM invoices WHERE total > 100)
    TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv);

-- Common options: FORMAT (text | csv | binary), DELIMITER, NULL,
--   HEADER, QUOTE, ESCAPE, ENCODING, FREEZE, DEFAULT

-- Gotchas
-- * Server-side FROM 'file' reads on the database server and needs
--   privileges (superuser or pg_read_server_files).
-- * From a client, use psql's \copy, which streams via the client.
-- * COPY FROM is a single command: if any row errors, the whole
--   command fails (newer versions have ON_ERROR options).
-- * Constraints, triggers and indexes still apply to loaded rows.
-- * COPY works on tables (and views for TO via query), not
--   arbitrary relations for FROM.
-- * Client libraries expose it via the copy protocol
--   (e.g. COPY ... FROM STDIN).
pg-easy-65.title: Bulk loading with COPY

pg-easy-67.syntax:
-- General forms
nextval(regclass)  -> bigint
currval(regclass)  -> bigint
lastval()          -> bigint
setval(regclass, bigint [, is_called boolean]) -> bigint

-- Example setup
CREATE SEQUENCE order_no START 100 INCREMENT 5;

SELECT currval('order_no');      -- error if nextval not yet called in this session
SELECT setval('order_no', 500);  -- next nextval returns 505
SELECT setval('order_no', 500, false); -- next nextval returns 500
SELECT lastval();                -- latest value returned by nextval in this session, any sequence

-- Typical use
INSERT INTO orders(id, item) VALUES (nextval('order_no'), 'pen');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence state is shared by all sessions; currval/lastval are session-local.
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are not rolled back
--   on ROLLBACK, so gaps in values are normal.
-- * Concurrent sessions each receive distinct values, never blocked by
--   other transactions' uncommitted calls.
-- * CACHE n makes a session preallocate values; other sessions may see
--   out-of-order values.
-- * Argument is regclass: a quoted name, resolved via search_path;
--   use 'schema.seq' to be explicit.
-- * serial / identity columns use a sequence behind the scenes.
pg-easy-67.title: Sequence manipulation functions (nextval, currval, lastval, setval)

pg-easy-68.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_name [INCREMENT BY n] [START WITH n] [CACHE n] [CYCLE];
SELECT nextval('seq_name');   -- advance and return the new value
SELECT currval('seq_name');  -- last value nextval returned in THIS session
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100);         -- set current value explicitly
SELECT setval('seq_name', 100, false);  -- next nextval returns 100

-- Example
CREATE SEQUENCE invoice_no START 500;
CREATE TABLE invoice (id bigint DEFAULT nextval('invoice_no'), note text);
INSERT INTO invoice (note) VALUES ('first');

-- Gotchas (as comments)
-- * Sequence operations are non-transactional: they are designed so that
--   concurrent sessions never block each other on nextval.
-- * Consider how the effect of nextval interacts with transaction
--   commit/abort, and what that means for numbering continuity.
-- * Other causes of unused numbers: failed INSERTs, CACHE preallocation,
--   crash recovery.
-- * currval errors if nextval was not yet called in the session.
-- * serial / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY columns use sequences internally,
--   so they follow the same rules.
-- * Do not rely on sequences for gap-free numbering; use a separate
--   counter table with row locking if that is required.
pg-easy-68.title: Sequence functions: nextval, currval, setval

pg-easy-69.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE TABLE child_table (
  extra_col type, ...
) INHERITS (parent_table [, other_parent ...]);

-- Example (different names)
CREATE TABLE vehicles (id serial PRIMARY KEY, wheels int);
CREATE TABLE trucks (payload_kg int) INHERITS (vehicles);

INSERT INTO trucks (wheels, payload_kg) VALUES (6, 9000);

-- Querying a parent includes rows from its children by default
SELECT * FROM vehicles;        -- parent plus all descendants
SELECT * FROM ONLY vehicles;   -- parent's own rows only
SELECT * FROM vehicles*;       -- explicit 'include children'

-- Variations and gotchas (as comments)
-- * Child gets all parent columns, then its own; same-named columns are merged.
-- * Each table keeps its own storage; a row lives in exactly one table.
-- * CHECK and NOT NULL constraints are inherited; PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE
--   and FOREIGN KEY constraints and indexes are NOT.
-- * Parent-level UPDATE/DELETE also affect child rows unless ONLY is used.
-- * Later ALTER TABLE on the parent propagates to children.
-- * Add/remove link later: ALTER TABLE t INHERIT p; / NO INHERIT p;
-- * Dropping the parent needs CASCADE if children exist.
-- * CREATE TABLE ... (LIKE p) copies columns only, with no link.
-- * Declarative partitioning (PARTITION BY) is usually preferred now.
pg-easy-69.title: Table inheritance (INHERITS clause)

pg-easy-70.syntax:
-- General form
-- column_name data_type [ DEFAULT default_expr ] [ constraints ]
-- default_expr is a value expression evaluated per row at INSERT time
-- whenever the column is not supplied (omitted or DEFAULT keyword).

CREATE TABLE ticket (
  id        BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  status    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  priority  INT DEFAULT 3,
  opened_on DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- Default applies: column omitted, or DEFAULT keyword used
INSERT INTO ticket (priority) VALUES (1);
INSERT INTO ticket (status, priority) VALUES (DEFAULT, 2);

-- Change or remove a default later (affects only future inserts)
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority SET DEFAULT 5;
ALTER TABLE ticket ALTER COLUMN priority DROP DEFAULT;

-- Gotchas
-- * An explicit NULL is stored as NULL; the default is NOT used.
-- * A default does not imply NOT NULL; add that constraint separately.
-- * A default is not applied by UPDATE (use a trigger for that).
-- * Volatile functions (random(), clock_timestamp()) run per row;
--   now() returns the current transaction's start time.
-- * Defaults cannot reference other columns or contain subqueries.
-- * Without DEFAULT, an omitted column becomes NULL.
pg-easy-70.title: Column DEFAULT expressions

pg-easy-71.syntax:
-- General form: a function call returning a value of type uuid
--   <function_name>()

-- Example: using a UUID generator as a column default
CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id    uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT <uuid_function>(),
    label text
);

INSERT INTO invoices (label) VALUES ('march') RETURNING id;

-- Call it directly in a query:
SELECT <uuid_function>();

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * The result has type uuid (128-bit), shown as 8-4-4-4-12 hex digits.
-- * Core Postgres (13+) provides gen_random_uuid() with no extension needed;
--   older versions needed the pgcrypto extension.
-- * Newer versions (18+) also add uuidv4() and uuidv7(); check the docs
--   for what each version-specific function guarantees.
-- * The uuid-ossp extension offers other generators, e.g. uuid_generate_v1(),
--   uuid_generate_v3()/v5() (namespace + name based).
-- * Each call is evaluated per row when used in DEFAULT or SELECT lists.
-- * The ordering of generated values affects index locality on a primary key.
pg-easy-71.title: Built-in UUID generation functions

docs.title: Packaging Related Objects into an Extension

pg-easy-72.syntax:
-- General form
CREATE EXTENSION [ IF NOT EXISTS ] extension_name
    [ WITH ] [ SCHEMA schema_name ]
              [ VERSION version ]
              [ CASCADE ];

-- Examples
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS hstore;
CREATE EXTENSION "uuid-ossp" SCHEMA public;

-- Notes / gotchas
-- * An extension is a packaged set of SQL objects (functions, types,
--   operators, etc.) defined by files already installed on the server
--   (the contrib/ package or OS package). CREATE EXTENSION does not
--   fetch or compile anything from the network.
-- * It acts on the CURRENT database only. Run it in each database
--   that needs the objects.
-- * IF NOT EXISTS: no error if already installed (a notice is issued);
--   it does not check that the installed version matches.
-- * If the extension's files are not on the server, you get an error
--   like: could not open extension control file.
-- * Usually needs sufficient privileges; trusted extensions can be
--   installed by non-superusers with CREATE on the database.
-- * CASCADE installs required dependent extensions too.
-- * Inspect: \dx   or   SELECT * FROM pg_extension;
--   Available: SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions;
-- * Remove: DROP EXTENSION name;  Upgrade: ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE;
pg-easy-72.title: Postgres extensions: CREATE EXTENSION

pg-easy-73.syntax:
-- General form (run inside psql, not as SQL):
--   \d<letter>[S+] [pattern]
-- The letter after \d picks the kind of object to list.
-- Suffix + adds more detail (size, description, etc.).
-- Suffix S includes system objects.
-- pattern is an optional name filter; supports * and ?.

-- Examples:
--   \dv+ report_*     -- views whose names start with report_, with detail
--   \dT               -- user-defined data types

-- Common letters in the family:
--   \d name   describe one relation (columns, indexes)
--   \dt       tables
--   \dv       views
--   \di       indexes
--   \ds       sequences
--   \dn       schemas
--   \df       functions
--   \du       roles
--   \dT       data types
--   \dE       foreign tables
--   \l        databases (not a \d form)

-- Gotchas:
--   * Letters are case-sensitive: \dt and \dT differ.
--   * Meta-commands are psql features, not server SQL;
--     they work by querying the system catalogs.
--   * Use psql -E to echo the SQL a meta-command runs.
--   * Another letter in this family covers installed
--     extensions; check \? for the full list.
--   * Without a pattern, only objects visible on the
--     search_path are listed for many kinds.
pg-easy-73.title: psql describe meta-commands (\d family)

pg-easy-74.syntax:
-- General form (tag is optional):
--   $tag$ ...text... $tag$
--   $$ ...text... $$
-- Content between the delimiters is taken literally; the opening and
-- closing tag must match exactly.

-- Examples:
SELECT $$Line one
line two$$;

SELECT $q$Contains $$ inside and a path C:\temp$q$;

-- Typical use: function bodies
CREATE FUNCTION add_one(i int) RETURNS int AS $body$
BEGIN
  RETURN i + 1;
END;
$body$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Variations and gotchas:
-- * Standard string: 'text' (a literal quote is written as '').
-- * Backslashes are not treated as escapes inside dollar quotes.
-- * Tags are case-sensitive and cannot start with a digit.
-- * Tags let you nest: use different tags for the outer and inner quoting.
-- * No parameter or variable substitution happens inside the body.
-- * A $ directly after an identifier is part of that identifier,
--   so separate the opening tag from a preceding name with whitespace.
-- * Plain 'strings' can also span multiple lines.
pg-easy-74.title: Dollar-quoted string constants

pg-easy-75.syntax:
-- General form
INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2, ...)
VALUES (expr, expr, ...) [, (expr, expr, ...) ...]
[ON CONFLICT ...]
[RETURNING output_expr [, ...]];

-- Example: a VALUES list with several parenthesized tuples
INSERT INTO pets (name, age)
VALUES ('Rex', 3), ('Mia', 5)
RETURNING name, age;

-- Example: DEFAULT and omitted columns
INSERT INTO pets (name, age)
VALUES ('Bo', DEFAULT);

-- Notes / gotchas:
-- * Each parenthesized tuple in VALUES describes one row.
--   Tuples are separated by commas.
-- * Every tuple must have the same number of expressions,
--   matching the column list; otherwise Postgres raises an error.
-- * Columns not listed in the column list get their default
--   (or NULL if no default).
-- * Multi-row VALUES is a single statement: it succeeds or
--   fails as a whole.
-- * VALUES can also be used standalone as a table expression:
--   SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'x'), (2,'y')) AS v(id, label);
-- * Alternative: INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... inserts rows
--   produced by a query.
pg-easy-75.title: INSERT with a VALUES list

pg-easy-76.syntax:
-- General form of the command family
-- Statements begin with a command keyword. Postgres has several
-- besides SELECT: VALUES, WITH, TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ...

TABLE name;
-- TABLE is a documented SQL command, not just a clause
-- (see the SELECT reference page, section "TABLE Command").

-- Example with a different table:
TABLE customers;

-- Variations: TABLE can be used wherever a SELECT query can be,
-- and can take trailing clauses such as ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET:
TABLE customers ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 5;

-- Usable as a subquery or source:
WITH c AS (TABLE customers) SELECT count(*) FROM c;
INSERT INTO customers_archive TABLE customers;

-- Gotchas:
-- * It takes only a table name (optionally schema-qualified,
--   and ONLY / * inheritance forms), not column lists or WHERE.
--   For filtering or choosing columns, use a full SELECT.
-- * psql meta-commands such as \d are client features, not SQL.
-- * Locking is controlled by LOCK or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE,
--   not by naming a table in a query.
-- * Compare the sibling command: VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b');
--   which also stands alone as a query.
pg-easy-76.title: Postgres TABLE command and statement starters

pg-easy-77.syntax:
-- General form
VALUES (expr [, ...]) [, ...]
    [ ORDER BY sort_expr [ASC | DESC] [, ...] ]
    [ LIMIT count ] [ OFFSET start ];

-- Example: used as a row source in FROM, with aliases for table and columns
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES (10, 'x'), (20, 'y'), (30, 'z')) AS t(num, label)
WHERE num > 10;

-- Example: used in INSERT
INSERT INTO items (id, name) VALUES (1, 'pen'), (2, 'ink');

-- Notes and gotchas
-- * VALUES is a command in its own right, not only part of INSERT.
-- * Every row must have the same number of columns.
-- * Without aliases, columns are named column1, column2, ...
-- * Column types are resolved across all rows (like UNION);
--   incompatible types raise an error.
-- * In FROM, the VALUES list must be in parentheses and needs an alias
--   if you want to name its columns.
-- * Can be used in CTEs: WITH v(a, b) AS (VALUES (1, 2)) SELECT * FROM v;
-- * Row order is not guaranteed unless you add ORDER BY.
pg-easy-77.title: VALUES lists in PostgreSQL

pg-easy-78.syntax:
-- General form
SELECT unnest(array_expression);
SELECT * FROM unnest(array_expression) [WITH ORDINALITY] AS t(col [, ord]);

-- Example: text array used in FROM, with position numbers
SELECT t.letter, t.pos
FROM unnest(ARRAY['x','y']) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(letter, pos);

-- Example: expand an array column, keeping other columns
SELECT id, unnest(tags) AS tag FROM posts;
